title: The small catechism
hook: Luther wrote a simple Q&A for families: what does this mean?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm 46 and the hymn Luther built on it. Your line was a river, and a stillness. When something shook today, which did you reach for, the walls or the stillness? Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

A small booklet, open on a table at home. A parent reads a line out loud: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." Then the parent asks a question, the same question the booklet asks after almost every line: what does this mean? And a child answers, in a sentence short enough to remember. That's the scene Martin Luther wrote for. In the preface to his Small Catechism, he describes going around the parishes and being shocked at what he found: ordinary people who barely knew the Lord's Prayer or the commandments, and pastors who couldn't teach them. His answer wasn't a thicker book. It was a thinner one. Today's word: catechism.
screen: `NOT A THICKER BOOK. A THINNER ONE.`

segments.voice: A catechism is a teaching book, usually set out in questions and answers, for learning the basics of the faith. Luther also wrote a larger one for pastors. The small one has a note at the top of each part: this is how the head of a household should teach it, simply, to the family. So the classroom he had in mind was a home. The Small Catechism walks through the Ten Commandments, the Apostles' Creed and the Lord's Prayer, then baptism, confession and the Lord's Supper. And after each piece comes the same short question: what does this mean? Here's how plain the answers get. The first commandment, no other gods. What does this mean? In Luther's answer, we should fear, love and trust God above all things. That's it. One breath. Or take the Lord's Prayer, "Give us this day our daily bread." What does daily bread mean? Luther's answer is a long list that sounds like a household inventory. It includes food and drink, clothing and shoes, house and home, fields and cattle, money and goods, a faithful spouse, good government, good weather, peace, health, good friends and faithful neighbors, and the like. Shoes and good weather, inside the Lord's Prayer. The question does something on its own, too. It assumes the words you've said over and over might still be closed to you, and it invites you to open them. Lutheran churches still teach with it. Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed Christians have catechisms of their own, each with its own questions and its own answers. But the small question Luther kept repeating is one anyone can borrow.

Here's the practice: ask what does this mean? Choose one line you've said or heard so often it slides past. A line of the Lord's Prayer. A verse from yesterday's psalm. A blessing your family says before meals. Even a saying a grandparent used to repeat. Say it once, slowly. Then ask the catechism's question and answer it in one plain sentence of your own. If you pray, you can end by saying the line again as a prayer. If you don't, just let your one sentence sit. The bell holds the time.
Catechism. A teaching book of questions and answers on the basics of the faith. Luther's small one was written to be taught at home.

Your line: what does this mean? Today, when you catch yourself saying a familiar phrase, at church, at work or at the dinner table, ask the question once, and answer it plainly. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Lutheran churches use Luther's Small Catechism to teach children and adults, especially before confirmation; Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches teach with catechisms of their own.

notes: Claims rule: no date for the catechism given. The preface's account of the visitation (people and some pastors not knowing the Lord's Prayer, Creed or Commandments) is paraphrased; confirm wording.
The heading 'as the head of the family should teach them in a simple way to his household' is paraphrased; confirm.
The daily-bread list is paraphrased from Luther's explanation of the Fourth Petition; confirm the items (including shoes, good weather, faithful neighbors).
The order of parts (Commandments, Creed, Lord's Prayer, Baptism, Confession, Lord's Supper) is given as in common editions; confirm.
'Lutheran churches still teach with it' and the line about Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed catechisms are general knowledge, not from a cited text; confirm or trim.
Word 'catechism' defined without an etymology, per the claims rule.

Editor pass: removed the counts 'Luther wrote two' and 'four words'; marked the daily-bread list as partial ('and the like'); changed 'kitchen inventory' and the practice's 'explain it to a child at the table', which repeated day 855's practice.

Second editor pass: the preface now says ordinary people barely knew the prayers and pastors couldn't teach them (Luther's complaint about pastors is incompetence, not ignorance of the Lord's Prayer); hook and fork no longer say 'kitchen table' (repeated from 855); the daily-bread list is introduced as 'it includes', since several of Luther's items are left out.
